summary: Specifies how to use the Session Description Protocol to describe the configuration of the FEC Framework between sender and receiver. It includes examples of grouping multiple source and repair flows.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6364 defines the SDP attributes that describe Forward Error Correction settings. Before media flows, a sender can use a session description to say which flows carry the original packets, which flow carries the repair packets, and how long a receiver should wait for repair packets. A receiver that reads the description knows how to rebuild lost packets.

questions: how to describe fec in sdp
what is the sdp repair-window attribute
subtitle: How a sender and a receiver describe Forward Error Correction settings in a session description.

tldr.problem: A sender that protects media with Forward Error Correction must tell the receiver which flows carry source and repair packets, which FEC scheme is in use, and how long the receiver should wait. The FEC Framework does not say how to encode that information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6364 defines the SDP attributes that carry the FEC Framework configuration: fec-source-flow, fec-repair-flow and repair-window, plus the FEC/UDP and UDP/FEC transport protocol identifiers and the existing grouping attributes.
tldr.outcome: A sender and a receiver can exchange FEC settings in an ordinary SDP description, including cases with several source flows and several repair flows. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6364 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2011, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It defines the SDP binding for the FEC Framework described in RFC 6363.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The FEC Framework, described in RFC 6363, is a general framework for recovering lost packets in media streams. It does not need continuous signalling between sender and receiver. It does need a set of parameters exchanged once, at the start, so both sides agree on the FEC configuration.

SDP, the Session Description Protocol, is a simple text format for describing multimedia sessions. RFC 6364 introduces the SDP elements that Content Delivery Protocols built on the FEC Framework use to carry the FEC Framework Configuration Information. The document also gives examples that show how several source flows and repair flows are grouped together when an application uses more than one FEC Framework instance.
sections.plainLanguage: Forward Error Correction lets a receiver rebuild a lost packet from repair packets sent alongside the media. Both sides must agree in advance on which flows carry what, and on the FEC scheme. RFC 6364 says how to write that agreement into an SDP session description.

sections.title: FEC and the FEC Framework
sections.content:
FEC groups source packets into blocks and applies protection to those blocks to generate a desired number of repair packets. The repair packets can be sent on demand or independently of any receiver feedback, depending on the FEC scheme, the Content Delivery Protocol, the loss characteristics of the network, the transport scheme, and the application. At the receiver, lost packets are recovered by erasure decoding, provided that a sufficient number of source and repair packets arrived.

The FEC Framework defines the common components of Content Delivery Protocols and the requirements for FEC schemes used within them. It deliberately leaves out the details of any one scheme. It does not say how repair packets are generated and used, and it does not say how the configuration information travels between sender and receiver. Those are left to the individual FEC schemes and Content Delivery Protocols.

The FEC Framework Configuration Information is the minimum set of data the sender and receiver need. It identifies the repair flows, defines each source flow that a repair flow protects, names the FEC scheme, gives the length of the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID in octets, and carries zero or more FEC-Scheme-Specific Information elements, each a name and a value whose valid names and ranges the FEC scheme defines.
sections.plainLanguage: Forward Error Correction groups media packets into blocks, then sends extra repair packets for each block. If some packets are lost, the receiver rebuilds them from the packets it has. The FEC Framework in RFC 6363 sets out the common parts of that job and leaves the scheme-specific details to each FEC scheme. This RFC covers only the step where both sides agree on the settings.

sections.title: SDP Elements
sections.content:
Two new transport protocol identifiers are defined. FEC/UDP names the case where a FEC scheme takes a UDP-formatted input stream and appends an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID to produce a source flow. UDP/FEC names the FEC repair packet format. If a FEC scheme does not use the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID, the original transport protocol identifier must be used instead, so that receivers without FEC support still work.

The SDP group attribute, with the FEC grouping semantics, associates source and repair flows. The SDP source-filter attribute expresses the source addresses or fully qualified domain names in the FEC Framework.

Source flows are described with the new fec-source-flow attribute. Its id parameter is required and must be an integer; the identifier is unique among all source flows protected by the same FEC repair flow. The optional tag-len parameter gives the length of the Explicit Source FEC Payload ID in octets. It must be present when that field is used and must be absent when it is not. A source flow identifier need not be carried in source packets, because the packets are tied to their flow by their own headers.

Repair flows are described with the new fec-repair-flow attribute. Its required encoding-id parameter names the FEC scheme that produced the repair packets; these identifiers are in the range 0 to 255 and are registered by IANA. The optional preference-lvl parameter gives the order in which repair flows should be used. If it is absent, the receiver may use the repair flows in any order. The optional ss-fssi and fssi parameters carry the FEC-Scheme-Specific Information as comma-separated name:value elements. Information needed only by the sender goes in ss-fssi; everything else goes in fssi. If the FEC scheme needs no specific information, neither parameter may be present.
sections.plainLanguage: The new SDP attributes carry the settings. The fec-source-flow attribute numbers each protected media flow and states the length of the extra source identifier field. The fec-repair-flow attribute names the FEC scheme, gives an optional order for using several repair flows, and carries the scheme-specific settings as name:value pairs. Grouping attributes tie the repair flow to the source flows it protects.

sections.title: The Repair Window and Bandwidth
sections.content:
The repair window is the time that spans a FEC block, which consists of the source block and the corresponding repair packets. At the sender, the FEC encoder processes a block of source packets, generates repair packets, and transmits both the source and the repair packets within a duration no larger than the repair window value. The window therefore limits the maximum number of source packets that can be included in a FEC block.

At the receiver, the FEC decoder should wait at least for the duration of the repair window after the first packet of a block arrives, so that all repair packets have a chance to arrive. The decoder may begin decoding packets it already has sooner, but it should not report a decoding failure before that wait is over. The waiting time can be adjusted when packets are missing at the start of the block.

The repair-window attribute gives the size in milliseconds (ms) or microseconds (us). It is a media-level attribute, because each repair flow may have a different window. A window given as an absolute time does not necessarily match an integer number of packets or the clock rate used in RTP, which can cause mismatches between successive windows, though the RFC notes that in practice this does not break the decoding process.

The bandwidth specification is optional. It can express the bandwidth of the repair flows or of the session. When it is present, the RFC recommends the Transport Independent Application Specific (TIAS) bandwidth modifier and the maxprate attribute, unless the Application-Specific (AS) modifier is used. AS is not recommended, because TIAS allows the bitrate to be calculated according to the IP version and transport protocol while AS does not. In TIAS-based calculations the packet size includes all headers and payload but excludes the IP and UDP headers; in AS-based calculations it also includes the IP and UDP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The repair window is the time span of one FEC block. The sender must send the original and repair packets of a block within that time, and the receiver should wait that long before declaring a block unrecoverable. The repair-window attribute states the length in milliseconds or microseconds. A longer window allows larger blocks but delays recovery.

sections.title: Session Announcement and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
In a multicast application, the sender may advertise the FEC Framework Configuration Information for all the protection options it offers as part of a session announcement. Each receiver then chooses the protection it wants from one or more FEC Framework instances and subscribes to the corresponding multicast sessions to receive the repair flows. Unless the Content Delivery Protocol requires it, receivers should not send an answer back, because that can overwhelm the sender in large-scale multicast applications.

In a unicast application, a sender and receiver may use the Offer/Answer Model. The sender offers the options available to that particular receiver, and the receiver answers with its choices. Receivers that support the SDP Capability Negotiation Framework may also use that framework to negotiate all or a subset of the FEC Framework parameters. Backward compatibility in the Offer/Answer Model is handled as specified in RFC 5956.
sections.plainLanguage: How the settings are exchanged depends on the application. In multicast, the sender lists what it offers and each receiver picks what it wants without replying, because replies would flood the sender. In unicast, the sender offers and the receiver answers, and the receiver may also negotiate a subset of the parameters.

sections.title: SDP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four example scenarios. In the first, one source video flow S1 and one repair flow R1 form one FEC group with the line a=group:FEC-FR S1 R1. The source and repair flows go to the same port on different multicast groups, and the repair window is 150 ms.

The second example has two source flows, S2 and S3, protected by one repair flow R2 in the group a=group:FEC-FR S2 S3 R2, with a repair window of 150500 us. The third has two source flows, S4 and S5, each protected by its own repair flow, R3 and R4, in two separate groups, with repair windows of 200 ms and 400 ms. The fourth has one source flow S6 protected by two repair flows, R5 and R6, in two groups, both with a repair window of 200 ms and with different preference levels, so that the receiver knows which repair flow to use first.

The RFC notes that the mid attribute of RFC 5888 identifies a media stream with a token, while the identifiers for source flows are integers. Using the same values for both is not recommended, even when the mid values are integers, because it is ambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the attributes combine. One source flow with one repair flow is the simplest case. Two source flows can share a single repair flow, two source flows can each get their own repair flow, and one source flow can be protected by two repair flows with different preference levels so the receiver knows which to use first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC calls the threat weak: a modified SDP that shows an incorrect association or grouping of the source and repair flows can cause FEC protection to fail, or cause other media streams to be mishandled. It recommends that the receiver perform an integrity check on the SDP so that it trusts only SDP from trusted sources, and that the receiver also follow the security considerations of SDP in RFC 4566. For the use of source address filters in SDP, the reader is pointed to the security considerations in RFC 4570. The security considerations for the FEC Framework itself also apply, as detailed in RFC 6363.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is that someone changes the session description so that the receiver pairs the wrong repair flow with the wrong media flow. The receiver is advised to check the integrity of the description and to trust only descriptions from sources it trusts.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document updates the Session Description Protocol (SDP) Parameters registry defined in Section 8.2.2 of RFC 4566. It adds the values FEC/UDP and UDP/FEC to the table for the proto field.

It also registers three new SDP attribute names: fec-source-flow, whose purpose is to provide parameters for a FEC source flow; fec-repair-flow, whose purpose is to provide parameters for a FEC repair flow; and repair-window, whose purpose is to indicate the size of the repair window. All three are media-level attributes, are not subject to charset restrictions, and take their values from this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two transport protocol names and three SDP attribute names are added to the IANA registries, so that the same words mean the same thing for every implementation.

viz.caption: ABNF of the two new flow attributes (RFC 6364)

data.title: fec-source-flow and fec-repair-flow
data.code:
fec-source-flow-line = "a=fec-source-flow:" SP source-id
     [";" SP tag-length] CRLF

source-id = "id=" src-id
src-id = 1*DIGIT ; Represented as 32-bit non-negative
                 ; integers, and leading zeros are ignored

tag-length = "tag-len=" tlen
tlen = %x31-39 *DIGIT

fec-repair-flow-line = "a=fec-repair-flow:" SP fec-encoding-id
     [";" SP flow-preference]
     [";" SP sender-side-scheme-specific]
     [";" SP scheme-specific] CRLF

fec-encoding-id = "encoding-id=" enc-id
enc-id = 1*DIGIT ; FEC Encoding ID

flow-preference = "preference-lvl=" preference-level-of-the-flow
preference-level-of-the-flow = 1*DIGIT
